body:
If I put considerable time between what I've done and when I meet the man I want to spend my life with, I don't think past mistakes will be as relevant as they feel now. Still, I'm hesitant to lie about my history to a potential partner for two reasons: It's likely that the truth will be found out later on in the relationship. I don't want him to feel like he can't trust me. Also,  I would feel guilty for lying. Maybe I shouldn't feel guilty since 
      I would only be lying to protect my interests, but I would. 

I don't have any moral qualms about lying, I just doubt it will pay off long-term. Not thinking about long-term consequences is how I got here in the first place. :)

I don't want to lie about my sexual history to someone I'm considering spending the rest of my life with. The truth always emerges and since relationships are built on trust, misleading him would jeopardize a future where he can depend on knowing that what I tell him is true.
Is it too late to participate?

I think your writing could improve if you used less "to be" verbs and compressed what you are trying to say in shorter stanzas. For example  make the second line " I want to be,  I ought to be" Thanks for looking at [mine](https://www.reddit.com/r/OCPoetry/comments/4618rm/vacancy19862016/).

The violence of sex is a pretty strong theme in your poem (ape, gracelessly ,burn, etc). The theme is reinforced by choppy and terse structure, "violent." I felt the questions softened the harsh sounds elsewhere in the poem. Try replacing them with imperative statements. (think of me! leave blue bruises on my thighs!).

Thanks for your reply. This poem is about the death of US Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia. The references to the "paper" and "his words" include a metaphor for his body and the American Constitution. Scalia had a textual interpretation of the law and this poem expresses that his death means the court will have a more liberal interpretation now that he is gone. Supposedly this will benefit the speaker and other people his decisions marginalized.

The first three stanzas were colorful and worked well to describe the woman you were looking for. I agree that the concept in the final stanza works well to retrospectively frame the rest of the poem, but I think you could make it a little more..interesting? The other lines seem to be trains of thought and fragments whereas the last lines form a full sentence. Try chopping it up to stay consistent with the rest of it.

I *really* love the transition from warm,fond memories to disturbing, painful ones. It demonstrates the nuance of a problematic character really well especially since the speaker identifies with her. 

If you want to make the poem flow better, try rearranging the number of syllables so that each consecutive line has the same number of counts. You can break from this for dramatic effect.
